title: GPU pool drain orchestration & capacity-safe rollout tooling
creator: Sophie Klein
description:
Goal: Ship a safe, observable, and automatable workflow for upgrading Dedicated GPU pools that prevents capacity outages during rolling upgrades. This ticket covers the orchestration primitives and rollout gates we need: coordinated autoscaler handoff, graceful GPU drain semantics, preflight capacity verification against active commitments, canary window policies by LTS channel, and automatic rollback triggers on SLO regressions.

Problem statement:
- Upgrades to runtime or kernel-level components require draining GPU nodes/pools. Drains can spike queue depth and latency if autoscalers react poorly or if in-flight KV cache warmups are lost.
- Current process is manual: engineers cordon pools, manually migrate traffic, and monitor dashboards. This is error-prone for multi-pool upgrades and bursts.

Proposed design:
1) New primitives:
   - drain-controller: a controller that implements cordon -> graceful evict of inference workers -> tracked KV cache snapshot/warmup hook -> uncordon after post-checks.
   - scale-plan: calculates temporary capacity reservations (buffer) using active route commitments, 95p token throughput estimates, and historical autoscaler response latency.
   - fleetctl upgrade: cli to orchestrate per-cluster, per-pool upgrades with LTS channel selection and rollback windows.

2) Rollout policy / gates:
   - LTS channel-aware canaries: minor patches go to "lts-stable" pools first; major runtime bumps go to "lts-canary" with extended monitoring.
   - Preflight gate: verify scale-plan can provision buffer capacity in target region within 10 minutes against peak 30-day observed bursts.
   - Runtime health gate: after draining and restarting N nodes, require no SLO regressions for 15 minutes before proceeding to next batch. Gate metrics: 95th latency, error-rate, queue-depth, GPU-utilization, and request-drop-rate.
   - Autoscaler coordination gate: momentarily switch autoscaler to 'maintenance mode' for target pools so it does not aggressively downscale in response to transient traffic shifts; revert automatically post-upgrade.

3) Eviction and KV cache handling: 
   - Add a 'kv-warmup' lifecycle hook: before evicting a worker, snapshot top-N recent KV keys for active customers and prepopulate a warmup job on new nodes. This reduces cold-cache amplification on pooled capacity.
   - Soft-evict for in-flight batches: allow active requests to finish but prevent new long-running requests to be scheduled onto draining nodes.

4) Routing and fallback: 
   - Temporary traffic routing rules to divert a configurable percentage of traffic to cross-region or public fallback pools during each batch.
   - Quota-aware admission: refuse new large-batch requests if scale-plan cannot satisfy them within SLO window.

5) Rollback & safety:
   - Automatic rollback on SLO breach: if any gate metric crosses the configured threshold for >3 minutes during a gate window, mark upgrade as failed and run fleetctl rollback which reverts pool images and re-runs warmup on previous nodes.
   - Postmortem metadata captured automatically and attached to the ticket and the Confluence runbook.

Telemetry and observability:
- New dashboards: "Upgrade Health" per-cluster showing gate state, buffer utilization, downstream route errors, KV-warmup hit ratio.
- Tracing hooks to tag requests impacted by an upgrade wave for easier sampling and debugging.
- SLO alerting thresholds documented in runbook.

Implementation notes and trade-offs:
- Implementing kv-warmup increases network and storage IO; we limit warmup to top-N customers and only for LTS channel upgrades where regression risk is high.
- Temporarily switching autoscalers to maintenance mode reduces responsiveness to unrelated failures; hence we only enable it per-pool and only for the duration of the drain gate with a strict upper time limit.
- We accept a small, controlled cost of overprovisioning (buffer) during upgrades in exchange for predictable latency.

Artifacts and references:
- Confluence spec: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/DIY-Upgrade-Orch
- Draft runbook: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/Upgrade+Runbook
- Dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/upgrade-health/cluster-overview
- Related PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/6243, https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/6310

Acceptance criteria:
- drain-controller can drain a small pool (<=8 GPUs) with KV-warmup enabled without triggering P99 latency regressions above 20% in 80% of trials (test harness).
- scale-plan produces a reservation plan and can validate buffer capacity automatically against live autoscalers.
- fleetctl can perform a one-click canary rollout to a defined LTS channel and support automatic rollback.
- Runbook and dashboards are published and reviewed by SRE and Release Engineering.

Next steps:
- Spike: implement minimal drain-controller prototype and validate kv-warmup hook (owner: Rajiv).
- Run load tests in staging to calibrate buffer sizing heuristics (owner: SRE team).
- Iterate on gate thresholds after 2 weeks of canary observations.
